summary.summary: Bristol's 2024/25 treasury outturn shows long-term debt rising to £600m (average rate 4.56%) against treasury investments of just £55m, lifting net debt by £118m to £545m — the first year of a five-year strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing to fund the capital programme. The council remains substantially under-borrowed against its £969m capital financing requirement (CFR, the underlying need to borrow), funding the gap from cash rather than loans, and it complied with every treasury limit; general-fund financing costs were a moderate 7.18% of net revenue. Two watch items stand out: the £165m of new PWLB (Public Works Loan Board) debt was taken very short (about 1.2-year average life), so £70m — 12% of the book — matures within twelve months and must be rolled, and lenders called two LOBO loans in-year, the council repaying £35m at par rather than accept resets near 5.9%, leaving £35m of LOBOs (lender-option loans) at medium call risk.

signals.headline: Net debt up £118m to £545m and total borrowing to £600m in 2024/25 as £165m new PWLB drawn
signals.why: Debt is climbing at the start of a strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing over 2024-2029.

signals.headline: £165m new PWLB (Feb-Mar 2025) taken at ~1.2yr average life; £70m (12%) of debt matures within 12 months at 31 Mar 2025
signals.why: A concentrated near-term maturity wall that must be refinanced at whatever rates prevail on maturity.

signals.headline: Lenders called LOBO options in-year: £10m Dexia (05/12/2024) and £25m Commerzbank (24/02/2025) repaid at par vs ~5.9% resets; £35m LOBOs remain at medium call risk
signals.why: A called LOBO is repaid at par, as both of these were. The remaining £35m is therefore a refinancing and liquidity exposure — cash to repay and funding to replace — not a rate-reset one.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Maintained schools deficit balances increased to 24 schools (up from 21), with nursery sector crisis: 11 of 12 nursery schools in deficit totalling £5.5m.
findings.detail: The number of schools in cumulative deficit rose from 21 to 24 during 2025/26. Nursery schools are the critical issue: 11 of 12 maintained nursery schools are in deficit with a combined shortfall of £5.5m. The paper notes "some of these deficits represent a substantial proportion of their annual budgets". While the team reduced deficits by £0.9m during 2025/26, this was insufficient to prevent the position deteriorating.
findings.matters: Schools in deficit pose governance risk and may eventually require council bailout or closure. The concentration in nursery provision suggests either demographic pressure or unit cost issues. This is a leading indicator of broader DSG sustainability problems filtering down to maintained school sector.
findings.figures: 24 schools in deficit (up from 21), 11 of 12 nursery schools in deficit, £12.2m cumulative school deficits, £5.5m nursery deficit
findings.quote: Out of 24 schools sharing the end of year cumulative deficit position of £12.2 million, the nursery sector continues to be a concern, with 11 out of 12 maintained nursery schools in a deficit position which totals £5.5 million. Some of these deficits represent a substantial proportion of their annual budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Corporate property portfolio generated £1.6m rental income shortfall, including £0.6m loss at 100 Temple Street alone.
findings.detail: Property management deteriorated by £1.6m against revised budget, with £1.4m of this from rental income shortfalls across multiple corporate properties. 100 Temple Street commercial lettings underperformed by £0.6m. This is separate from issues at Bottle Yard Studios and other cultural venues, and reflects broader challenges with the commercial estate.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is volatile and the council is over-reliant on it. Large income shortfalls at key assets (100 Temple Street) suggest either market deterioration or property condition/management issues. These are discretionary income sources that support core service delivery through charging recharges.
findings.figures: £1.6m property management deterioration, £1.4m rental income shortfall, £0.6m at 100 Temple Street
findings.quote: Property Management deterioration of £1.6 million driven by rental income shortfall across multiple properties of £1.4 million despite enhanced income from City Point, £0.1 million additional spend on external fees supporting commercial estate rental income and £0.1 million shortfall on income due to voids and rent concessions granted due to suitability.
